title_guess: Lending-rate systems in India: PLR, BPLR, base rate and MCLR, and why monetary policy transmission stayed weak
recurring_cast: timeline header: yellow band across the top, a blue 1973-2003 'prime lending rate' bar, then ticks that gain labels per reform (2003 BPLR, 2010 base rate, 2015 weak-transmission note, 2016 MCLR)
bank_building (small pink-roof bank icon), alone, in a row of four, or with a gold ring when singled out
person (black standing customer at the right end of a 'loan' arrow)
percentage_badge (blue % signs on deposit and borrow lines; % tags on customers)
RBI 'monetary policy' to bank 'lending rates' arrow pair, reused for 2015 and for the MCLR test
running_examples: PLR panel: one bank, four customers tagged 5%, 15%, 12%, 3% (negotiated rates; never spoken)
BPLR = rate charged to the most creditworthy customer (tag 5%), assumed to be the minimum
2010 report: lending below BPLR shown as 77%
Jan 2015 - April 2016: repo cut 1.25%, lending rates down only 0.6%
funds loop: depositors and other banks/RBI supply money, each paid interest, so funds have a cost to the bank

best_moments.why: under BPLR, dotted arrows rise from the RBI coin into a pink 'FIXED' box of four banks; under base rate (148.4) the arrows run the other way, from the banks down to RBI, beside 'banks can fix their own base rate'. Regulation vs deregulation is the direction of one set of arrows
PLR in one panel: one bank facing four customers, each holding a different % tag; negotiated, non-standard rates are visible without a sentence
weak transmission as two numbers on one line: '1.25% ↓' under RBI's policy, a long dotted arrow, then only '0.6% ↓' under the bank's lending rates

funds loop: a crowd of depositors sends 'deposit' into the bank, 'other banks / RBI' send 'borrow', and two blue % lines loop back out labelled 'cost to bank' while the bank sends 'loan' to a customer: why lending rates follow funding costs

two small calculation trees side by side under the timeline: base rate takes only a deposit % into 'cost of funds'; MCLR takes deposit % and borrow % into 'marginal cost of funds', and the borrow % gets a ring tagged 'depends on repo & tenure'
the RBI-to-bank arrow inside a blue frame turns red and dotted, 'transmission improved?' gets a red 'NOT MUCH', then a big handwritten 'But why?' closes on an open question

weak_moments.why: verify before reuse: the picture and narration say RBI fixed every bank's BPLR ('FIXED' box); BPLR is usually described as set by each bank under RBI guidance

verify before reuse: 'marginal cost of funds' is explained as deposits plus borrowings versus 'cost of funds' as deposits only; the usual meaning of marginal is the cost of new (incremental) funds against an average cost
three more criteria (minimum rate of return, cost of maintaining CRR, operating expenses) appear as green text lists on both sides and are never spoken ('seen in the previous video')

verify: the timeline starts the prime lending rate system in 1973; the 1.25% repo cut is tied to 'Jan 2015 - April 2016' (a window that, by common accounts, saw a larger cut); the 77% report is placed at 2010
the customer tags 5%, 15%, 12%, 3% and the 5% for the best customer are shown but never spoken; a learner may read them as real rates

segments.teaches: recall: from 1973 to 2003 banks followed the prime lending rate (PLR) system and could lend to customers at any rate by negotiation, so the system had neither standardisation nor transparency

elements.what: yellow header band with a blue 1973-2003 bar labelled prime lending rate
bank icon
'PLR' over a light-blue panel
four customer figures in the panel, each with a green tag showing a different % (5, 15, 12, 3)
'issues with this system:' heading with two cream tags, lacking transparency and lacking standardisation

segments.notes: 5 change events (~every 7 s). The % tags are an unspoken picture of negotiation.
segments.idea: under PLR each bank bargained a different rate with each customer, so nobody could compare or check rates
segments.shown_as: a timeline bar marks 1973-2003 as the PLR era; a bank icon is joined in a blue PLR panel by four customers, each holding a different % tag; under it 'issues' writes on with two tags, lacking transparency and lacking standardisation

segments.teaches: in 2003 RBI brought in BPLR: each bank was asked at what rate it lends to its most creditworthy customers, and that rate was taken as its benchmark prime lending rate

elements.what: BPLR and its full name hang from the 2003 tick
bank at left, one customer at right with a 5% tag
arrow bank → customer labelled 'most creditworthy customer'
blue circle around the customer's 5%, a line to an 'interest rate' label
band: benchmark prime lending rate = interest rate

segments.notes: 5 change events in 18 s (~every 3 s): the fastest stretch. The customer and tag appear about 4 s before 'most creditworthy' is said.
segments.idea: BPLR is the rate a bank charges its best borrower
segments.shown_as: BPLR drops from the 2003 tick; the PLR panel clears to one bank and one customer holding a 5% tag; an arrow labelled 'most creditworthy customer' runs to him, his 5% is circled and linked to 'interest rate', and a band writes 'BPLR = interest rate'

segments.teaches: RBI fixed all banks' BPLRs and so regularised lending rates, assuming that BPLR was the minimum rate and no bank would lend below it, to bring transparency and standardisation; neither came, and BPLR as a minimum proved an assumption

elements.what: four bank icons in a pink box headed BPLR with a red '[FIXED]' tag
RBI coin below with four dotted arrows rising to the banks
'BPLR = minimum interest' beside a wavy brace
transparency and standardisation tags
red crosses under both tags
'BPLR = minimum interest' struck through, red 'proved to be an assumption' written beside

segments.notes: 6 change events (~every 9 s). Verify: whether RBI 'fixed' BPLRs (usually each bank set its own under guidance).
segments.idea: RBI set a benchmark for every bank and assumed it was a floor, hoping for clear, uniform rates; the floor was only an assumption
segments.shown_as: four banks sit in a pink box stamped FIXED while dotted arrows rise to them from the RBI coin; 'BPLR = minimum interest' writes beside a brace with the two goals as tags; red crosses fall under both goals, then the equation is struck and 'proved to be an assumption' is written in red

segments.teaches: a 2010 RBI report found banks were giving more than 77% of their loans below BPLR, so RBI changed policy at once and brought in the base rate system in 2010

elements.what: new 2010 tick on the header
report icon with an orange tick under the 2010 tick
'total bank lending below BPLR rate = 77%' line beside the report
'BASE RATE' label under the 2010 tick

segments.notes: 4 change events (~every 4.5 s). 77% is on screen about 4 s before it is spoken; screen says 'total lending 77% below BPLR', speech says 'almost all banks lend over 77% of loans below BPLR'.
segments.idea: evidence showed most lending happened below the supposed floor, which ended BPLR
segments.shown_as: a 2010 tick grows on the timeline; a report icon with a tick drops under it and writes 'lending below BPLR = 77%', then the report gives way to a 'BASE RATE' label on the 2010 tick

segments.teaches: base rate is the rate below which a bank cannot lend to any customer (loans at or above it); each bank sets its own and tells RBI, so rates were deregulated; this time transparency and standardisation were achieved

elements.what: pink box: interest rate below which a bank cannot lend, with four bank icons inside
gold rings around single banks (first one, then another)
'lending rates (>= base rate)' arrow from the ringed bank to a customer
'banks can fix their own base rate' line into the left bank
RBI coin below; dotted arrows now run from the banks down to RBI
transparency and standardisation tags, then blue ticks

segments.notes: 10 change events (~every 4.4 s). The same pink box and RBI coin as in BPLR, but the arrows reverse: banks report to RBI instead of RBI fixing banks. The same two goal tags return, now ticked.
segments.idea: under base rate each bank sets its own floor and reports it, and every loan must be at or above it
segments.shown_as: the pink box now reads 'rate below which a bank cannot lend'; one bank gets a gold ring and sends 'lending rates >= base rate' to a customer; a second bank is ringed with 'banks can fix their own base rate'; dotted arrows run from the banks down to the RBI coin; the transparency and standardisation tags return and get blue ticks

segments.teaches: in 2015 RBI found monetary policy transmission weak: a change in the policy (repo) rate should show in banks' lending rates; from Jan 2015 to April 2016 repo was cut 1.25% but lending rates fell only 0.6%

elements.what: 'weak monetary policy transmission' box on a new 2015 tick
RBI coin labelled monetary policy, '[repo rate]' under it
bank labelled lending rates
arrow from monetary policy to lending rates
pale band 'Jan 2015 - April 2016': '1.25% ↓' then a dotted arrow to '0.6% ↓', both red down-arrows
'weak monetary policy transmission' under a blue line, then red 'BUT WHY?'

segments.notes: 6 change events (~every 11 s). Verify the figure for the window: the cut is usually given as 1.25% for 2015 and larger up to April 2016.
segments.idea: a repo cut is meant to pass through to loan rates; only about half of it did
segments.shown_as: a 'weak transmission' note hangs from a new 2015 tick; the lower canvas clears to the RBI coin (monetary policy, repo rate) with an arrow to a bank (lending rates); a band below writes the window, '1.25% ↓' under RBI, a long dotted arrow, and only '0.6% ↓' under the bank; a blue line underlines 'weak monetary policy transmission' and a red 'but why?' follows

segments.teaches: the reason: repo rate was not part of the base rate calculation, so repo changes did not move base rates, on which lending rates depended; in 2016 RBI introduced MCLR, whose calculation includes repo

elements.what: '[calculation]' under base rate, dotted to red '[repo rate not considered]'
new 2016 tick labelled MCLR with its own '[calculation]'
green '[repo rate is considered]' under MCLR

segments.notes: 5 change events (~every 7 s). The lower RBI-bank picture fades as the MCLR tags appear: the answer replaces the problem. Red vs green tag is the whole contrast.
segments.idea: transmission was weak because the floor rate ignored repo; MCLR was built to include it
segments.shown_as: under 'base rate' a '[calculation]' tag drops a dotted line to a red 'repo rate not considered'; a 2016 tick grows with 'MCLR [calculation]', and as the RBI-bank picture fades, a matching tag under MCLR reads in green 'repo rate is considered'

segments.teaches: banks get loanable funds from depositors (savings, current and term deposit accounts) and by borrowing from other banks or RBI; both cost interest, so funds have a cost to the bank, and a higher cost means a higher lending rate

elements.what: bank with a 'loan' arrow to a customer
dark crowd of depositors with a 'deposit' arrow into the bank, 'savings / current / term deposit accounts' under it
'other banks / RBI' with a 'borrow' arrow into the bank
two blue elbow lines with % marks looping from the bank back to depositors and to other banks/RBI
red 'cost to bank' labels on both loops
blue underline under base rate [calculation] on the timeline

segments.notes: 11 change events (~every 5.6 s). Built in story order: loan out, deposits in, borrowing in, interest back out, cost named. 'Cost to bank' appears about 5 s before 'cost' is said.
segments.idea: the money a bank lends is not free: it pays interest to depositors and lenders, and that cost sets its lending rate
segments.shown_as: the lower canvas clears to a bank sending a 'loan' arrow to a customer; a crowd of depositors sends 'deposit' into the bank from the left, 'other banks / RBI' send 'borrow' from above, then blue % lines loop back out from the bank to each source and both loops are tagged 'cost to bank'
segments.example: deposits (savings, current, term) and borrowings from other banks or RBI, each paid interest

segments.teaches: base rate was calculated from the cost of deposits only (cost of funds); MCLR counts the cost of both deposits and borrowings (called here the marginal cost of funds), hence 'marginal cost of funds based lending rate'

elements.what: under base rate: a 'deposit' line down to a blue %, then a dotted line to 'cost of funds'
under MCLR: 'deposit' and 'borrow' lines to two blue %s that join in a V to 'marginal cost of funds'
blue underlines under each [calculation] tag
MCLR label widens into a blue box with its full name

segments.notes: 5 change events (~every 12 s). Verify the meaning of 'marginal': the video equates it with adding borrowings; it usually means the cost of new funds.
segments.idea: the old rate looked at one source of funds, the new rate at both
segments.shown_as: the funds picture clears; under base rate one 'deposit' line drops to a %, which feeds 'cost of funds'; under MCLR a 'deposit' line and a 'borrow' line drop to two %s that meet in a V and feed 'marginal cost of funds'; the MCLR tag then stretches into a blue box spelling out the full name

segments.teaches: borrowing cost depends on repo (so on RBI's policy) and on tenure (repo, term repo and long-term operations carry different rates), so MCLR adds a tenor premium; the other three inputs (minimum return, cost of CRR, operating expenses) are the same as for base rate

elements.what: yellow ring on the borrow % with an arrow to 'depends on repo', later '& tenure'
'tenor premium' added under marginal cost of funds
green three-item lists (minimum rate of return, cost of maintaining CRR, operating expenses) under both sides

segments.notes: 3 change events in 58 s (~every 19 s): slow, list-like stretch. The three green items are never spoken.
segments.idea: MCLR is linked to repo through the borrowing cost and adds a premium for longer tenure; the rest of the recipe is unchanged
segments.shown_as: the borrow % gets a yellow ring with an arrow to 'depends on repo', then '& tenure'; 'tenor premium' writes under MCLR's cost list; finally the same three green items write under both trees so the only differences left are the borrow line and the tenor premium

segments.teaches: from 2016 MCLR became each bank's minimum lending rate; a loan's rate = MCLR + a spread the bank sets by tenure, credit risk and so on, never below MCLR

elements.what: 'depends on repo' under the MCLR box
bank labelled lending rates
'[MCLR + spread]' under lending rates

segments.notes: 2 change events in 32 s. Spread is a label only; no number example.
segments.idea: loan rate = MCLR floor + the bank's own spread
segments.shown_as: the calculation lists clear, leaving 'depends on repo' under MCLR; a bank icon labelled lending rates appears with '[MCLR + spread]' written under it

segments.teaches: the test: after MCLR, did repo changes show in lending rates? Some improvement, but not enough; strong transmission was still not achieved, so why, and what did RBI do next?

elements.what: RBI coin, monetary policy [repo rate], arrow to the bank's lending rates
light-blue frame around the RBI-bank pair
'monetary policy transmission improved?' under a blue line
the RBI-bank arrow turns into a red dotted arrow
red 'NOT MUCH'
large handwritten blue 'But why?' at right

segments.notes: 6 change events (~every 7 s). The solid arrow becoming a weak red dotted one is the verdict in motion. The next system is not named.
segments.idea: MCLR helped a little, but repo changes still did not pass fully into loan rates
segments.shown_as: the RBI coin (monetary policy, repo rate) returns with an arrow to the bank's 'MCLR + spread'; a blue frame closes round them and 'transmission improved?' writes underneath; the arrow turns into a red dotted line, 'NOT MUCH' appears in red, and a big hand-lettered 'But why?' pops in at the right

segments.teaches: channel end card (next video, playlist, app promotion); not teaching

elements.what: next-video and playlist panels with bird illustrations; an app promotion banner slides in

segments.shown_as: canvas cuts to a two-panel end card
